title: Failure
hookLine: Peter, Paul, David, Moses all failed badly

cards: A short list of résumés. One man killed someone and fled the country. One took another man's wife, then arranged for the husband to die in battle.
One went house to house dragging believers off to prison. One promised he would never deny his friend, and then did, before the cock crowed. Moses.
Scripture writes these moments down in plain sight. And none of their stories stops there.

teach.h: PETER WEPT, AND WAS SENT BACK.
teach.b: Peter's story has a strange order.
Before the denial, Jesus tells him in Luke: "I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren." The comeback is spoken before the fall.
Then Peter denies him, and "Peter went out, and wept bitterly." Later, by the sea in John's Gospel, the risen Jesus asks him, "Lovest thou me?" and gives him a job: "Feed my sheep." Then David.
Nathan the prophet tells him of a rich man who steals a poor man's only lamb. David is furious. Then Nathan says it: "Thou art the man."

David answers, "I have sinned against the LORD." The heading of Psalm 51 ties it to this moment: "Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me." The story is honest that consequences stay.
But it keeps going. Then Moses, whose running you met in year two. He killed a man and ran to Midian.
And it was there, keeping someone else's sheep, that the bush burned and the call came.

teach.h: THE CALL FOUND A MAN WHO RAN.
teach.b: The call found a man who had run. Last, Paul. He never pretends the past didn't happen: "I am the least of the apostles, that am not meet to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God."

teach.h: BY THE GRACE OF GOD I AM WHAT I AM.
teach.b: Then the next sentence: "But by the grace of God I am what I am." Failure is not final doesn't mean failure didn't matter. Peter wept.
David's house suffered. But in each story, the failure is a chapter, and the book goes on.

how: Christians bring their failures to God in confession, privately or in a service, and Catholic and Orthodox Christians also confess to a priest and receive absolution; Psalm 51 is used as a prayer of repentance in several liturgies.

o: falling short, sometimes badly, with the story going on
a sin that scripture quietly leaves out of its heroes
the end of any chance of being used by God

games.q: failure in scripture — tap the pairs.

s: the Bible hides its heroes' failures
David's sin, Peter's denial and Paul's persecution of the church are all written down plainly.
Paul calls himself the least of the apostles
because I persecuted the church of God. but by the grace of God I am what I am.
Moses was called at the burning bush before he ever failed
he had killed a man and fled; the call came while he kept sheep in Midian.

games.q: you're Peter. you denied Jesus three times. now the risen Jesus is on the shore asking, lovest thou me? what does he do next?
o: give you a job: feed my sheep.
games.why: he asks, and each time gives Peter work: feed my lambs, feed my sheep. the one who failed is sent to care for others.

practice: Choose one failure you keep replaying, one that still stings, and name it the way Paul named his: this happened, and it was mine. If you can still make it right, set that aside for later; for now, put down the punishment.
If you pray, say David's line, create in me a clean heart, O God; if you don't, tell yourself plainly: that was a chapter, not the end.
If it ever turns into thoughts of harming yourself, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Failure. Falling short, sometimes badly. In scripture Moses, David, Paul and Peter all fail, and every one of their stories keeps going.

orig.note: Hebrew: I have sinned — David's answer to Nathan in 2 Samuel 12:13.

carryVoice: Your line: failure is not final. Peter wept, and then was given a job. Until tomorrow.
